# Conti Ransomware Leaks and Public Attribution Record

## Executive Summary

Public reporting describes Conti as a large, commercially organized ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation rather than a small, informally coordinated criminal group. The available record depicts a division of labor between malware developers, testers, reverse engineers, administrators, penetration testers, affiliates, and outside providers. Its business model relied on double extortion: operators stole data, encrypted victims’ systems, demanded payment, and threatened to publish or sell the stolen information if victims refused. ([S1](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/); [S3](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

The February–March 2022 Conti leaks materially strengthened public understanding of that structure. The leaked chats reportedly contained 393 JSON files and approximately 14 megabytes of communications, including discussions of hiring, salaries, product development, security testing, phishing, infrastructure, and internal finances. Rapid7 assessed that the scale of the material suggested access by a senior insider or a coalition of disgruntled affiliates, although that assessment was not presented as a proven identification of the leaker. ([S2](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

The attribution record is strongest at the organizational level and more limited at the individual-alias level. Rewards for Justice characterizes Conti, also known as Wizard Spider, as a Russian government-linked RaaS group and identifies the online aliases “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis” as Conti-linked malicious cyber actors. That page does not provide a public real-name mapping between those aliases and the defendants named in the Department of Justice record. ([S1](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/))

The Department of Justice record directly identifies five defendants in two federal cases involving alleged Conti-related conduct: Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, Andrey Zhuykov, and Oleksii Lytvynenko. The record states that the first four were charged with conspiracy to violate the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and conspiracy to commit wire fraud, while Lytvynenko was charged with conspiracy to deploy Conti and later pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud. The record also expressly preserves the presumption of innocence for defendants who have not been adjudicated guilty. ([S4](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2))

My assessment is that the evidence supports a well-founded description of Conti as a professionalized RaaS enterprise with a distributed workforce and affiliate model. It also supports a distinction between (1) public intelligence assessments about Conti’s Russian links and aliases, and (2) judicially documented allegations or proceedings involving named defendants. The sources do not establish that the five defendants were the individuals operating the aliases listed by Rewards for Justice.

## Sources and Evidentiary Weight

| Source ID | Source | Principal evidentiary contribution |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | Rewards for Justice, U.S. Department of State | Official reward notice, aliases, organizational attribution, victimology, malware associations, and alleged Russian government linkage |
| S2 | Rapid7 | Analysis of the 2022 chat leaks, Conti’s operations, technical development, infrastructure, and political dispute |
| S3 | Center for Internet Security | Analysis of Conti’s commercialization, departments, staffing, affiliate relationships, and operational budgeting |
| S4 | U.S. Department of Justice, Middle District of Tennessee | Case numbers, defendant names, charges, procedural posture, and Lytvynenko’s reported guilty plea |

The sources have different purposes. The DOJ and Rewards for Justice pages are government records, but their statements must still be read according to their legal or programmatic context. An indictment or charging notice records allegations, not final factual findings. A reward notice identifies persons of interest and investigative targets, not necessarily convicted individuals. Rapid7 and CIS provide expert or institutional analysis of leaked material, but they are secondary interpretations rather than court findings.

## Conti as a Ransomware-as-a-Service Operation

### Business model and double extortion

Conti is described as a RaaS operation in which the core organization developed and maintained ransomware while affiliates or other operators conducted intrusions. CIS explains that RaaS groups lease malware or access to affiliates, who perform attacks and share proceeds with the developers. The article gives an illustrative profit division of approximately 70–30, although the supplied material presents that ratio as a common RaaS arrangement rather than necessarily a proven universal Conti payment rule. ([S3](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

The operational objective was double extortion. Conti operators typically exfiltrated victims’ files and encrypted servers and workstations. Victims were directed to an online portal to negotiate payment, and nonpayment could result in publication or sale of the stolen data. Rewards for Justice reports that ransom demands varied widely and could reach $25 million. ([S1](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/))

The victim profile included critical infrastructure and public-sector organizations. Rewards for Justice states that Conti ransomware was used in more than 1,000 operations against U.S. and international critical infrastructure and that more than 400 organizations worldwide were victimized, including more than 290 in the United States. The DOJ page separately states that Conti affected more than 900 businesses, nonprofits, governments, and other victims worldwide. These figures should not automatically be treated as inconsistent: they may reflect different counting methods, time periods, or definitions of “operation,” “organization,” and “victim.” ([S1](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/); [S4](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2))

### Affiliates and initial access

The RaaS model reduced the need for the core organization to conduct every intrusion itself. CIS reports that affiliates could obtain or use established access supplied by initial access brokers, allowing the core group to scale attacks while shifting operational risk to affiliates. This structure also allowed developers to concentrate on improving the malware and related tooling. ([S3](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

Rapid7 reports that phishing was a common initial-access method and that Conti discussed phishing templates, third-party malicious-document providers, and methods for delivering ransomware without triggering dynamic analysis. The article also states that the leaked control panel showed compromised hosts and information such as operating systems, antivirus products, user rights, and infected assets. ([S2](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

The sources identify several tools and malware associated with Conti. Rewards for Justice lists Conti ransomware-as-a-service, TrickBot, IcedID, Cobalt Strike, and ZLoader as associated malicious applications. Rapid7 lists vulnerabilities that Conti was known to exploit, including EternalBlue-related vulnerabilities, ZeroLogon, PrintNightmare, Log4Shell, and ProxyShell/ProxyLogon vulnerabilities. ([S1](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/); [S2](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

## What the Leaks Revealed About Internal Structure

### Specialized departments

The leaks exposed an organization that resembled a software company in its division of labor. CIS reports that Conti used “Coders” to write and integrate malicious code, “Testers” to evaluate ransomware against security products, “Administrators,” “Reverse Engineers,” and “Penetration Testers/Hackers.” Spamming functions were reportedly contracted externally. Each department had its own budget, although units could borrow funds from one another. ([S3](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

CIS further reports that an insider described more than 60 employees in July 2021, mostly coders and testers. The workforce was not static: personnel could be dismissed after internal security breaches. This is significant because it supports the conclusion that Conti had durable administrative processes, personnel management, and internal security concerns rather than merely ad hoc cooperation among independent criminals. ([S3](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

### Recruitment, compensation, and product development

Rapid7 describes internal discussions involving technical interviews, coding exercises hosted on public repositories, salary negotiations, leave or out-of-office messages, and product status. These details support the characterization of Conti as a commercially managed organization. The existence of recruitment and compensation processes does not, by itself, establish a legally incorporated entity; it does demonstrate organizational behavior resembling a business. ([S2](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

The group also invested in product testing and development. CIS reports that Conti allocated approximately $60,000 to obtain a valid Cobalt Strike license, spent several thousand dollars per month on security and antivirus software for testing, and redirected reverse-engineering efforts toward Windows 11. Rapid7 similarly reports efforts to obtain endpoint-detection demonstrations and modify malware to evade detection. ([S3](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization); [S2](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

### Financial scale and possible state contacts

Rapid7 reports that the leaked chats identified a primary Bitcoin address that allegedly held more than $2 billion as of February 28, 2022. Because the article characterizes this as information revealed by the chats, and because the supplied source does not provide an independently verified blockchain analysis, the figure should be treated as a reported leak-derived estimate rather than an established audited balance. ([S2](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

Rapid7 also reports a conversation that allegedly indicated Russian Federal Security Service involvement in some funding and an interest in files relating to Bellingcat and Alexei Navalny. The source presents this as an indication within the leaked communications, not as a judicially proven finding. Rewards for Justice uses the broader formulation “Russian government-linked,” which is an official attribution assessment but does not publicly establish the precise nature of governmental control, direction, funding, or tasking. ([S2](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/); [S1](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/))

## Political Conflict, Leaks, and Organizational Disruption

The leaks followed Conti’s public declaration of support for the Russian government after Russia’s February 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Rapid7 reports that some Conti members supported Ukraine, creating internal conflict. Two days after the initial statement, Conti reportedly revised its message, condemning the war while threatening retaliation if Russian critical infrastructure were attacked. ([S2](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

The disclosure began on February 27, 2022, when the account known as “ContiLeaks” released a large archive of internal chats. Rapid7 reports that the archive included approximately 14 megabytes of material across 393 JSON files, although some messages were encrypted and unreadable. Additional files appeared on February 28 and March 1, including usernames, passwords, alleged server-access details, screenshots, communications, and a purported ransomware source-code file. Rapid7 expressly states that its team did not access remote systems using the exposed credentials and recommended against doing so. ([S2](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

The initial disruption did not immediately end Conti’s operational capacity. Rapid7 observed infrastructure takedowns after the disclosure but reported a resumption of normal operations by March 9, 2022. CIS later states that the larger Conti platform shut down in May 2022, rebranding into smaller units, and that its leak and negotiation infrastructure shut down about a month later. These accounts can be reconciled as a progression: short-term operational recovery after the leak, followed by a later dismantling or fragmentation of the larger public-facing platform. ([S2](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/); [S3](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

## Aliases and Public Attribution

Rewards for Justice identifies five aliases—“Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis”—as malicious cyber actors believed to be linked to Conti. The page associates them with Russia, Conti/Wizard Spider, and the Conti RaaS ecosystem. It does not state that these aliases correspond to any particular defendant in the Tennessee cases. ([S1](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/))

The same page offers up to $10 million for information leading to the identification or location of persons who, while acting at the direction or under the control of a foreign government, participate in malicious cyber activities against U.S. critical infrastructure in violation of the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. This is a reward program standard and investigative framing; it is not itself a criminal judgment against the aliases. ([S1](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/))

Accordingly, the public record supports the following cautious conclusion:

1. The aliases are officially treated as Conti-linked investigative subjects.
2. Conti is officially characterized as Russian government-linked.
3. The supplied sources do not establish the real identities behind the aliases.
4. The supplied sources do not connect “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” or “Dandis” by name to Galochkin, Rudenskiy, Tsarev, Zhuykov, or Lytvynenko.

## Law-Enforcement Records and Named Defendants

The DOJ Middle District of Tennessee page identifies two cases. Case number 3:23-CR-00092 names Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, and Andrey Zhuykov. The page states that they were charged with conspiracy to violate the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and conspiracy to commit wire fraud for their alleged roles in the Conti ransomware conspiracy. ([S4](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2))

Case number 3:23-CR-00088 names Oleksii Lytvynenko. The page states that he was charged with conspiracy to deploy Conti, a ransomware variant that infected computers and networks and encrypted data. It further reports that on June 10, 2026, Lytvynenko pleaded guilty to Count 2, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, pursuant to a plea agreement. The supplied page lists a September 10, 2026 sentencing date and states that the page was updated July 8, 2026. Because the supplied material does not report the outcome of sentencing, no conclusion about the sentence should be drawn. ([S4](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2))

The DOJ page states that defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt. That qualification is especially important for the four defendants whose listed charges are not accompanied in the supplied record by a conviction or guilty plea. Even for Lytvynenko, the plea is specifically described as applying to conspiracy to commit wire fraud; the supplied source does not state that every allegation in the charging narrative was admitted or adjudicated. ([S4](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2))

## Findings and Assessment

The evidence supports a coherent model of Conti as a professionalized RaaS organization. Its internal specialization, recruitment, budgeting, testing, affiliate relationships, and use of double extortion are mutually reinforcing indicators of commercialization. The leaks did not merely expose individual criminal conversations; they exposed organizational processes.

The evidence is less conclusive when moving from organizational attribution to personal attribution. Rewards for Justice provides aliases and a Russian location, while DOJ provides named defendants and charges, but the supplied sources do not bridge those two sets of identities. It would therefore be improper to state that any named defendant operated one of the RFJ aliases unless additional evidence were supplied.

Finally, the record describes Conti’s 2022 decline as fragmentation rather than a simple disappearance. Rapid7 observed continued operations shortly after the leak, while CIS later described the shutdown and rebranding of the larger platform. The most defensible interpretation is that the leak disrupted and ultimately contributed to organizational transformation, but did not instantly eliminate the underlying personnel, capabilities, or criminal relationships.

## References

Center for Internet Security. (n.d.). *The Conti leaks: A case of cybercrime’s commercialization*. CIS. [https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization)

Rapid7. (2022, March 1; updated May 9, 2024). *Conti ransomware group internal chats leaked over Russia-Ukraine conflict*. Rapid7. [https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/)

U.S. Department of Justice, U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Tennessee. (2026). *Conti ransomware*. [https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2)

U.S. Department of State. (n.d.). *Conti—Rewards for Justice*. [https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/)
